items.title: 3.3.2 Valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR)

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.2, printed pages 52-58 (Table 3.1, Figures 3.9 to 3.20), with Quick Checks 3.5 and 3.6 read in the self-check. No 3.3 or 3.3.1 is printed.

blocks.text: The VSEPR model describes the shapes of molecules from the electron pairs that surround the central atom. It was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940 and rests on the assumption that a molecule takes the shape in which the electronic repulsions among the valence electrons of the central atom are at a minimum. To have minimal repulsions the electron pairs arrange themselves at the farthest possible distances, and this arrangement determines the geometry of the molecule.

blocks.alt: Two molecules. SO3: sulfur double-bonded to three oxygens in a flat triangle with 120 degree angles. SO2: sulfur double-bonded to two oxygens with a lone pair on sulfur, so the molecule is bent and the O-S-O angle is a little less than 120 degrees.
blocks.caption: Shapes of multiply bonded molecules (SO3 and SO2) (original diagram after Figure 3.12).

items: Both the lone pairs (non-bonded) and the bond pairs take part in determining the geometries of molecules.
The electron pairs are arranged around the central atom so as to stay at maximum distance apart and avoid repulsions.

The electrons of lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs, so non-bonding pairs exert greater repulsive forces on bonding pairs and tend to compress them. The repulsions decrease in the order lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. An electron pair shared by two nuclei occupies less space than a lone pair bound by a single nucleus.
The two electron pairs of a double bond and the three of a triple bond contain a higher charge density but are regarded as single pairs.
Highly electronegative atoms on the central atom decrease the repulsions between the bond pairs but strengthen the repulsion by the lone pair.

blocks.text: The central atom is named A and the electron pairs around it B, giving molecules of the types AB2, AB3, AB4 and so on according to the valency of A. The electron pair geometry is determined by the total number of electron pairs around A, whereas the actual shape of the molecule is determined by the atoms, excluding the lone pairs. The steps are: choose the central atom, usually the least electronegative atom or the element with the fewest atoms (carbon in CCl4); count the electron pairs around it, bond pairs and lone pairs (four bond pairs and no lone pair in CCl4); read the electron pair geometry from the table (four pairs, tetrahedral); then give the shape, excluding any lone pairs.

blocks.caption: Geometries and shapes of covalently bonded compounds (Table 3.1)

blocks.text: In AB2 molecules the two electron pairs lie at 180 degrees, a linear geometry: BeCl2 has beryllium as the central atom with two bond pairs and no lone pair. In AB3 molecules three electron pairs lie at 120 degrees, a trigonal geometry: BF3 is trigonal planar with each F-B-F angle 120 degrees, and the hydrides of group 13, AlH3, GaH3 and BH3, are expected to be the same. In SnCl2 the tin atom has four outer electrons; it makes two bonds and keeps the other two as a lone pair which occupies one corner of the triangle, giving a distorted trigonal electron pair geometry in the vapour phase and a v-shaped molecule with an angle under 120 degrees. With multiple bonds, SO3 has all three regions occupied by S=O bonds and is perfectly trigonal at 120 degrees, while SO2 has a lone pair at one corner and a double bond at each of the other two, so it is angular like SnCl2.

In AB4 molecules the four electron pairs avoid each other by taking the corners of a regular tetrahedron with bond angles of 109.5 degrees. In methane each of carbon's four valence electrons pairs with the single electron of a hydrogen atom, and the four bond pairs point to the corners of a tetrahedron, a non-planar arrangement; every H-C-H angle is 109.5 degrees, and SiH4, GeH4 and CCl4 have the same shape. A tetrahedron has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles. In ammonia three atoms and one lone pair surround nitrogen; the lone pair reduces the ideal 109.5 degrees to 107 degrees and the molecule is a trigonal pyramid. Replacing hydrogen by electronegative atoms reduces the angle further: in NF3 the angles are compressed to 102.5 degrees, because the strong polarity of the N-F bond lets nitrogen pull the lone pair closer, which repels the bonding electrons more strongly, and because the bond pairs sit nearer the fluorine atoms, which weakens their mutual repulsion. Water is v-shaped with four electron pairs, two of them lone pairs at two corners of the tetrahedron; their greater repulsion reduces the angle to 104.5 degrees. Ions follow the same rules: the hydronium ion H3O+, formed when water captures a proton, is AB4 with one lone pair and is trigonal pyramidal like ammonia; the amide ion NH2- has two lone pairs and two bond pairs, a tetrahedral geometry and a bent (v) shape like water.

blocks.alt: Two panels. H3O+: oxygen bonded to three hydrogens with one lone pair above, four electron pairs in a tetrahedral arrangement giving a trigonal pyramidal shape. NH2-: nitrogen bonded to two hydrogens with two lone pairs, giving a bent (V) shape with an H-N-H angle of about 104 degrees.
blocks.caption: Shapes of hydronium (H3O+) and amide (NH2-) ions (original diagram after Figure 3.16).

blocks.text: In AB5 molecules the five electron pairs spread over the corners of a trigonal bipyramid: three positions in a planar triangle and two along an axis perpendicular to the plane, as in PCl5, with angles of 120 degrees within the plane and 90 degrees between an axial and a planar atom. Lone pairs change the shape more dramatically here. The tri-iodide ion I3- is linear although it is an AB5 system: the central iodine has five pairs, two bond pairs and three lone pairs, so its geometry is trigonal bipyramidal; the lone pairs take the three corners of the triangle and the two iodine atoms the apices above and below the plane, and excluding the lone pairs the shape is linear with the iodine atoms 180 degrees apart. In AB6 molecules six electron pairs take an octahedral geometry, four at the corners of a planar square and two on the perpendicular axis, with all angles 90 degrees, as in SF6. XeF4 is AB6 with four bond pairs and two lone pairs; the lone pairs stay farthest apart at 180 degrees, and excluding them the shape is square planar with all angles 90 degrees.

blocks.alt: Ten flat sketches of molecules: linear BeCl2, trigonal BF3, bent SnCl2 with a purple lone pair, tetrahedral CH4, pyramidal NH3 with one lone pair, bent H2O with two, trigonal bipyramidal PCl5, linear I3- with three lone pairs in the plane, octahedral SF6 and square planar XeF4 with two opposite lone pairs; a box lists the repulsion order.
blocks.caption: VSEPR geometries and shapes with their angles (original diagram after Table 3.1 and Figures 3.9 to 3.20).
blocks.long_description: Two pairs give a straight line at 180 degrees, three a flat triangle at 120 degrees, four a tetrahedron at 109.5 degrees, five a trigonal bipyramid at 120 and 90 degrees, and six an octahedron at 90 degrees. Lone pairs are counted for the geometry but not the shape, and because they spread wider than bond pairs they squeeze the bonds: NH3 to 107 degrees, H2O to 104.5 degrees, SnCl2 and SO2 below 120 degrees. Three lone pairs in the plane of a trigonal bipyramid leave I3- linear; two opposite lone pairs on an octahedron leave XeF4 square planar.
